job: Fresh graduate in computing and engineering
name: Ben Patel

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making the time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and what you really think. Tell me about a normal day right now.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I live with my parents above their corner shop, so my day starts with moving crates at seven, which is my rent. Then I'm at the counter or on my laptop by nine, sending applications and building small websites for local businesses, like a barber and a flower stall. I use an AI assistant for most of my coding and for tailoring every application.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What was the last stretch of study like, and what are you hoping for next?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I did software engineering and passed with an average mark. My final project was a rota app for a food bank where I volunteered, and they still use it. I had no internship because I was busy with volunteering and shifts, and about 90 applications later I've had no offer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one's called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say fine, but the tools I already use daily would be the same ones in ten years, which is a bit dull. Online I'd say a plateau is a chance for regulation to catch up before anything gets worse.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, it's still tough for me. Plenty of junior jobs ask for a first-class degree or an internship I never did, and AI hype or no hype that doesn't change. My family shop is quiet, and I'd feel I should be contributing more.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep the website side work going and try for ten clients, at maybe 150 each, which would cover a good part of my loan payments. I'd also contribute to an open source project to have something real on my profile, and apply to startups rather than big firms.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Restless more than scared. I know how to build things and I hate that it doesn't count yet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would count as proof for a startup?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Something that runs and someone uses, like the food bank rota app. I'd show them that and say I shipped it, with real users, in a real place.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What worries you when you picture the shop?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That it's slowly losing to the supermarket chain, and my parents are older. If I don't get a job, I'd end up working the till for years, and that's a trap I can see.

say: A plateau gives **regulation** a chance to catch up before things get worse.
The tools I use daily would stay the same, which is a bit **dull**.
think: Many junior jobs ask for a first-class degree or an **internship** I never did.
The family shop is quiet, and I feel I should **contribute** more.
do: Land **ten clients** for small websites at about 150 pounds each.
Contribute to an **open source** project and apply to startups, not big firms.
Keep working the shop counter and moving **crates** for rent.
feel: **Restless** more than scared, because I can build things and it doesn't count yet.
S0.quote: I know how to build things and I hate that it doesn't count yet.
fieldNote: Side income and shipped **projects** give him confidence that other graduates lack.
Worry centres on the **credential** gap, not AI.
The family **shop** is both a safety net and a trap he can see.

steps.text: Sign ten small businesses for 150-pound websites
Contribute code to an open source project this winter
Apply to startups instead of big firms
Keep working the shop counter for rent

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one's called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's what I'm already living. AI writes the first draft of code, tests, emails, and the people who know how to direct it will do the work of three. At work I'd say adapt quickly and share what you've learned.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I think the junior developer role as it exists is shrinking. Fewer firms want someone to write simple functions for a year while learning. But there's a spot for people who can build a whole small product with the tools, and I'm closer to that than most of my classmates.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd position myself as a one-person builder: a portfolio of three small products, real customers and a clear story about how I use AI. I'd go after small firms that want someone who can do the whole job. I'd also put about a third of my freelance money into a course on cloud and security.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Excited and a bit sick. The ground is moving, but I like moving ground.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You say you're closer to it than classmates. What does that rest on?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Daily practice. Most of my classmates avoid the tools because they think it's cheating or because they're afraid. I got used to them early, so I can finish a small app in a weekend.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who do you worry about?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My cousin Arun, who did a mechanical degree and applies to the same junior analyst posts. Arun doesn't use any of this. I try to show him, but he's stubborn.

say: AI writes the first draft of code and tests, so **adapt** quickly and share what you learn.
People who direct the tools will do the work of **three**.
think: The junior developer role as it exists is **shrinking**.
There is room for people who can build a whole small **product** with the tools.
do: Build a portfolio of **three small products** with real customers.
Target small firms that want someone who can do the **whole job**.
Spend a third of freelance money on a **cloud** and security course.
feel: **Excited** and a bit sick; the ground is moving, but I like moving ground.
S1.quote: There's a spot for people who can build a whole small product with the tools, and I'm closer to that than most of my classmates.
fieldNote: Treats AI as a **lever**, and sees early habit as his edge.
Still **anxious**, because the junior route he needs is shrinking.
Worries about a **cousin** who avoids the tools, a sign of social conscience.

steps.text: Build three small products with real paying customers
Take a cloud and security course with freelance money
Apply to small firms wanting a one-person builder
Show cousin Arun how to use AI tools weekly

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one's called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say governments must move on income support and training now, because two years won't be enough for them to write the rules. I'd also say, honestly, that people shouldn't panic, because panic doesn't help.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I'd be shaken. If AI does almost any thinking work better and cheaper, my skills, which are basically thinking work, are in the middle of the blast zone. My edge over classmates shrinks to almost nothing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stay where I am, keep earning from small clients while that's still possible, and save as much as I can, maybe 250 a month. I'd look for roles at companies building or deploying the AI itself, because those need people. I'd also ask my parents about reconfiguring the shop with ordering software, since someone will have to run it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Dizzy. Fast, exciting and awful at once.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said panic doesn't help. Are you panicking?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit, underneath. I notice I'm refreshing the news. But I give myself rules, like one hour of reading a day and then I build something.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do for the shop?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Put in an ordering and stock system, with a cheap tablet at the till. If robots come in three years, someone will deliver stock, but my parents still need to know what to order.

say: Governments must move on income support and **training** now, before two years run out.
Nobody should **panic** about it, because panic doesn't help anyone prepare.
think: My skills are basically thinking work, right in the **blast zone**.
My edge over classmates shrinks to almost **nothing**.
do: Keep earning from small clients and save about **250 a month**.
Look for roles at firms **building or deploying** the AI itself.
Set up an **ordering system** and a cheap tablet at my parents' shop.
feel: **Dizzy**: fast, exciting and awful at once.
S2.quote: If AI does almost any thinking work better and cheaper, my skills, which are basically thinking work, are in the middle of the blast zone.
fieldNote: Adaptive style gives him a **plan**, but he admits underlying panic.
Uses self-set **rules** to manage the news cycle.
Brings his **parents'** shop into the plan, linking family and income.

steps.text: Save 250 a month from freelance work
Apply to companies building or deploying AI systems
Set up an ordering and stock tablet at the family shop
Limit news reading to one hour then build something

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one's called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's the most important thing happening, and five years means we can still act: retraining funds, firms reporting what they automate, and safety rules. I'd say it online and at a local meet-up.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, five years feels like a real opportunity. If I get a good first job within the year, I'd have time to become someone who understands the systems, not just a coder. It's still risky, but I can steer it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd start something small of my own that uses the tools, like a booking service for local shops, and put hours in at nights. I'd apply to jobs and keep that going in parallel. I'd also spend a few hundred on a cloud certification and write publicly about what I'm learning.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Steady, with an edge. The deadline is a good push.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if your own business doesn't take off?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then I'll have a name and a track record for a job. I'm not betting everything on it, just using the time while I'm living at home and costs are low.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell people your age who aren't moving?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That waiting is the riskiest choice. I wouldn't lecture them, but I'd show them something I built and say it's not that hard.

say: Five years means we can still act: **retraining** funds and rules on what firms automate.
I'd say it online and at a local **meet-up**.
think: Five years feels like a real **opportunity** to become someone who understands the systems.
It is risky, but I can **steer** it.
do: Start a small **booking service** for local shops and work on it at night.
Spend a few hundred on a **cloud certification** and write publicly about what I learn.
feel: **Steady** with an edge; the deadline is a good push.
S3.quote: If I get a good first job within the year, I'd have time to become someone who understands the systems, not just a coder.
fieldNote: Sees the **deadline** as a push, a trait of adaptive people.
Plans a **second** income stream as a hedge, not a bet.
Low costs at **home** let him take risks others can't.

steps.text: Launch a booking service for local shops at night
Keep applying to junior developer jobs every week
Sit a cloud certification exam for a few hundred pounds
Write publicly about what he learns each month

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one's called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is generous, and people should treat it like a chance to design the transition properly, with unions, public funding and rules. I'd say I'm optimistic, but only if we use the time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Quietly, it's the one I'm least worried about. Ten years is a whole career's first act. I'd use it to grow the product skills, maybe start a company, and get my parents out of the debt they keep from the shop.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd take any decent job in the next year for wages and a reference, then keep building on the side. I'd save for a deposit and pay down my loan. I'd also help my parents bring the shop online and mentor people at the food bank on their first projects.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, and a bit keen. Ten years feels like a runway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does optimism depend on for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: On people not being left behind. I can be fine and still angry if my cousin Arun or the food bank volunteers get squeezed, because I know what that does to a family.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Anything that could still go wrong?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bad decade of hiring before the real change. I could end up at the shop till for years, and I'd lose the momentum I've built.

I'm optimistic, but only if we **use** the time.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The 2028 one, because the other four give me time to build and that gives me time to be useful. With two years I'd be doing it all in a panic with thin savings. What would help is quick income support, training that pays you while you learn, and some honesty from tech firms about what's coming.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Just that people tell me I'm lucky to use the tools. Using the tools isn't luck. I had the time, a family shop to live above, and parents who let me tinker. Not everyone does, and I'd like the system to notice.

headlineQuote: Using the tools isn't luck. I had the time, a family shop to live above, and parents who let me tinker.
portrait: Ben is a 23-year-old **software engineering** graduate with a pass, no internship and about 90 applications without an offer.
He lives above his parents' corner shop and earns a little from **website work** for local businesses.
He leans left, uses AI every day and sees early habit as his **edge** over classmates.
His mood runs from uneasy through **anxious**, to calm when ten years gives him a runway.
He thinks collectively, worrying about his cousin Arun and the **food bank** volunteers, as well as himself.
biggestWorry: The **2028** case, because he'd be building in a panic on thin savings.
whatWouldHelp: Fast **income support**, paid training and honesty from tech firms about what's coming.
